0: A general large model has solid knowledge question-answering ability, but in real enterprise use many questions involve internal product material, technical documentation, business policies and operating manuals. That knowledge is usually not part of the model's training data, and it keeps changing with the business.
2: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) offers a solution: before the large model answers, retrieve the content related to the question from the enterprise knowledge base, then give the retrieved results to the model to generate an answer.
3: The core idea of RAG can be summed up as: retrieve first, then answer. Traditional large-model question answering relies mainly on knowledge already learned in the model's parameters. For example, when a user asks a question, the model generates an answer directly from what it learned during training. RAG adds a knowledge-retrieval step: after the user asks, the system first looks up related content in an external knowledge base, then sends the question and the retrieved knowledge to the large model together, and the model combines them to produce the final answer.
4: A basic RAG flow can be written as: user question → knowledge retrieval → fetch related content → LLM generates the answer → return the result. RAG does not make the model relearn this knowledge; it temporarily supplies the reference material the current question needs.
6: RAG is not required for every large-model application, but it is very common in enterprise knowledge Q&A, smart customer service and document assistants.
7: If business knowledge has to keep being updated, RAG is usually the better fit. Enterprise product descriptions, business policies and operating standards may keep changing. Writing that knowledge into the model through training means retraining every time the knowledge changes, which is costly and hard to maintain.
8: RAG can update the external knowledge base directly. When a document changes, you only reprocess the relevant document and update the index; there is no need to retrain the whole model. RAG is also a good fit when answers need to cite sources: because the model's answer is generated from the retrieved documents, it can return the document name, section, page or the original passage alongside it, so users know where the answer came from.
10: RAG and fine-tuning can both improve a large model's performance in real business, but they solve different problems. RAG mainly solves “the model lacks the relevant knowledge”, while fine-tuning mainly solves “the model cannot complete the task as required”.
11: RAG does not change the model's own parameters. Before the model answers, it retrieves related content from an external knowledge base and gives that content to the model as the basis for the answer.
12: Fine-tuning is different. It further trains the model on specific training data and adjusts the model's parameters during training, so the model gradually learns how to handle a particular task. For example, the entity-recognition task mentioned in chapter 9 requires the model to output answers in a fixed format. When the task requirements change substantially, you usually need new training data and another round of fine-tuning.
13: In practice you can choose by the problem you need to solve: when you need to add or update knowledge, RAG fits better; when you need to change the model's task ability, output format or behaviour, fine-tuning fits better. The two can be combined. For example, fine-tuning can give the model question-answering or instruction-following ability, and RAG can then supply domain knowledge, so the model both completes the task as the business requires and answers from the latest domain knowledge.
15: A complete RAG system usually has two main stages: building the knowledge base and online question answering. Building the knowledge base turns raw material such as PDF, Word, Markdown and web pages into knowledge that can be retrieved. Online question answering looks up related content in the established knowledge base after the user asks. This experiment uses the publicly available Regulations on the Implementation of the Road Traffic Safety Law of the People's Republic of China as the document source, and builds a RAG system for road-traffic-safety questions.
17: Enterprise knowledge is usually scattered across PDF, Word, Excel, Markdown, web pages and other file types. Because their formats and internal structures differ greatly, before building a RAG knowledge base you usually convert these documents into unified, processable text or structured data. This process is called document parsing. For a RAG system, a good parsing tool should not only recognise the text but also recognise and preserve the original document's structure as far as possible — titles, paragraphs, tables, images, formulas and so on.
18: Many open-source tools can parse documents today; the more common ones include:
19: 1) MinerU is an open-source parsing tool for complex documents that converts PDF, images, Word, PPT and Excel into machine-readable formats such as Markdown and JSON. It recognises titles, body text, tables, images and formulas, and restores the document structure following human reading order as closely as possible, which makes it well suited as a document pre-processing tool in a RAG system: opendatalab/MinerU
20: 2) MonkeyOCR is a document-parsing project built on a multimodal model. It parses documents through structure recognition, content recognition and relation modelling, handles complex content such as text, tables and formulas, and supports Chinese and English documents. For PDFs with complex layouts where traditional text extraction performs poorly, this kind of vision-model parsing is worth considering: Yuliang-Liu/MonkeyOCR
21: 3) Dolphin is ByteDance's open-source document-image parsing model, which processes documents by “analyse first, then parse”. It identifies page layout and reading order first, then parses text, tables, formulas and code elements, which suits PDFs with complex layouts or scanned documents: ByteDance/Dolphin
22: 4) PaddleOCR is PaddlePaddle's open-source OCR and document-parsing toolkit. Besides the usual text recognition it offers layout analysis, table recognition and structured document parsing, turning content in PDFs and images into structured data better suited to later AI processing. For scanned PDFs, image documents and documents with a lot of Chinese text, PaddleOCR is a common choice: PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR
23: Different parsing tools have different strengths, and no single tool fits every document. When building a RAG system, choose according to document type, layout complexity, parsing accuracy and deployment cost.

29: After parsing, the long document must be split into smaller text pieces, usually called chunks. In a RAG system, embedding and retrieval work at the level of chunks, so sensible splitting improves later retrieval accuracy.
30: For the parsed Markdown, you can first split the content into paragraphs at blank lines, then merge adjacent paragraphs up to the configured chunk_size. When the content exceeds the given length, a new chunk is started.
31: To avoid losing context at the split points, you can also set chunk_overlap to keep a little repeated content between adjacent chunks. For example: chunk_size = 500, chunk_overlap = 50 means each chunk is about 500 characters and adjacent chunks keep about 50 characters of overlap. After splitting, you can store each chunk's id, content and file, which helps with vectorising, retrieving and locating the answer source later.

36: After splitting, you need to build a retrievable document store. Because a computer cannot retrieve directly by the meaning of natural language, you use an embedding model to turn each chunk into a vector. Embedding models map text into a high-dimensional vector space, where texts with closer meaning sit closer together. So after a user asks, you can turn the question into a vector too and compare it with the chunk vectors in the document store to retrieve the content semantically closest to the question.
37: The open community already offers several embedding models, such as BGE-M3 and Qwen3-Embedding. BGE-M3 is a multilingual embedding model from BAAI supporting over 100 languages and text input up to 8192 tokens. Compared with ordinary dense embedding models, BGE-M3 supports dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval at once, so it suits both the usual vector semantic retrieval and hybrid retrieval: FlagEmbedding.
38: Qwen3-Embedding is the Qwen team's series of text-vector models, built on the Qwen3 architecture and aimed mainly at text retrieval, clustering, classification and code retrieval. Qwen3-Embedding comes in 0.6B, 4B and 8B sizes to choose from according to quality and compute, and has good multilingual and long-text ability: Qwen3-Embedding.

43: The common vector-retrieval tools today include Faiss and Milvus. Faiss is Meta's open-source vector-similarity library, used mainly for efficient vector indexing and nearest-neighbour search. It is simple to deploy, needs no separate database service and can be used directly in a Python program, which suits learning, experiments and small-to-medium RAG systems. Milvus is a vector database for large-scale vector data; besides vector retrieval it offers data persistence, distributed storage, index management and several query capabilities, which suits larger data volumes and long-running, production deployments. Milvus is more complete than Faiss but also more involved to deploy and use.

49: Embedding models turn the user question and document chunks into vectors and retrieve by the distance or similarity between them. The advantage is that document vectors can be computed and stored in advance, so when the user asks, only the question vector needs computing and related content can be recalled quickly from a large set of documents. But this efficient retrieval has limits. The embedding model encodes the query and the chunk separately and computes relevance by comparing how similar the two vectors are in vector space. A reranker model matches interactively: it takes the query and a candidate chunk into the model together so the model analyses the relation between the two texts directly, which supports finer semantic matching.
50: So RAG systems usually use two-stage retrieval: embedding recall plus reranker reordering. First embedding quickly narrows a large set of chunks down to a batch of candidates, then the reranker makes finer relevance judgements and reorders that small batch. That keeps retrieval efficient while further improving the context quality given to the large language model.

60: After retrieval and reordering you have several chunks highly relevant to the user's question. Next, these become reference material submitted to the LLM together with the question. If the relevance meets the requirement, the retrieved content goes to the large language model to generate the answer; if the knowledge base holds nothing relevant enough, the system returns a refusal instead, so the model does not answer without grounds.

70: Once the RAG system is built, evaluation is still needed to judge whether the whole Q&A flow really works. Unlike ordinary large-model Q&A, a RAG result is affected by two stages at once: knowledge retrieval and answer generation. So RAG evaluation usually looks at both separately.
72: The criterion for the retrieval stage is whether the user's question can find its answer among the recalled chunks; the common metric is Recall@K. Recall@K is fairly intuitive: it measures how many relevant documents the top K results cover:
73: Recall@K: whether the correct document appears in the top K retrieval results.
74: \(Recall@K = \frac{\text{Number of relevant documents retrieved in the top K}} {\text{Total number of relevant documents}} \)
75: For example, if a question has 2 correct knowledge fragments and the top 5 results contain both, Recall@5 is 100%.
77: Retrieving relevant knowledge does not mean the final answer is correct; the LLM's output must be evaluated too. In the generation stage you can focus on answer correctness, completeness, relevance, citation accuracy and hallucination. See section 12.3 in chapter 12 for generation-metric details. These metrics show whether the model uses the retrieved knowledge accurately and reveal missing content, drift or unsupported statements. In practice, if retrieval is already accurate but generation still falls short, consider a stronger, larger model as the RAG generator to improve understanding and answering of complex questions.
